title: 'No one has to die like this again'; Clive Geddes inquest delivers sweeping recommendations to prevent jail suicides
article: Better training for police dealing with mentally ill people and an end to the use of segregation for suicidal or mentally ill inmates are among a list of 48 recommendations delivered by the jury at a inquest into the hanging death of Cleve Geddes at the Ottawa jail.

In their verdict delivered Monday, jurors also urged the Ottawa Carleton Detention Centre to create a specialized mental health unit "as soon as possible" and end the practice of doing psychological counselling through cell door meal hatches.
They also urged changes to the jail's phone system so that inmates can place calls to cellphones and not just land lines as with the current system.
The recommendations are non-binding but are meant to prevent another death like that of Geddes, who was found by guards unresponsive and hanging by a bed sheet in his cell.

Though Geddes died by asphyxiation, jurors ruled his death as "undetermined", meaning they couldn't decide whether he intended to end his life or hoped a hanging attempt would get him out of jail and into hospital to be treated for his paranoid schizophrenia.

But the most important recommendation for the Geddes family, said their lawyer, Paul Champ, was the last one: that the province proclaim into force the Correctional Services Reintegration Act, which prohibits the use of segregation for inmates who are suicidal or have mental illness.
The law received royal assent in May, but has not been enacted by the government, partly to allow jails time to do the renovations needed.

"The testimony we heard in this inquest about the appalling conditions of segregation was very difficult for everyone to hear. When we know it was a person who was mentally ill in that cell, I think that's what drove that recommendation," Champ said outside the inquest.
He said the Geddes family would continue to put pressure on the government and the agencies involved in his incarceration "to ensure that no one has to die like this again."

Over nine days of testimony, the five-person jury heard compelling, often heartbreaking testimony about how Geddes died and how he was passed from the Ontario Provincial Police to the court system to the jail to deal with.

The judge at his court appearance in Renfrew on a charge of uttering threats and assaulting police ordered him to hospital for a psychiatric assessment, but he ended up in jail because no beds were available.

"This is the first suicide inquest that I'm aware of that looked more broadly at what happened to the person, how they got to the jail in the first place," said Irene Mathias of Moms Offering Mutual Support, an advocacy group for families of the incarcerated.

"Each part of the system operates in a silo. They just pass the problem on to the next person. The police think, 'Oh, we'll just let the courts deal with it. And the courts, think, well, we'll just let the ROH (Royal Ottawa Hospital) and the jail deal with it."
Often information gathered at one stage isn't passed along, meaning every institution begins with a blank page, Mathias said.
"They don't know anything about the person. They don't know the circumstances of them being there. They don't know the history of their mental illness or what's going on in that person's life.
"That leads to bad decisions," she said. "They may be well-intentioned, but they're fatal."

Geddes said he was suicidal when he arrived at the OCDC after his arrest on Jan. 30, 2017 and spent much of his time on suicide watch and in segregation, wearing a stiff, canvas gown nicknamed a "baby doll" and confined to a cold cell for more than 20 hours a day.

He died just a day after he was transferred to the jail's maximum security B-Pod, against the advice of a jail psychologist who testified she thought he would do better around other people in one of the jail's dormitories.

Many of the jury's recommendations had been suggested by lawyers with legal standing at the inquest. But the jurors added a few of their own, including that the OPP, the Ministry of Health and Long Term Care, the Ministry of Community Safety and Correctional Services, The Royal and the OCDC get together to hold a joint review after every suicide in custody.

In his closing remarks, presiding coroner Dr. Michael B. Wilson made special mention of the testimony of Jai Robert Middleton, an inmate who knew Geddes on B Pod and warned jail staff that Geddes was seriously ill and needed to be in hospital.
Middleton testified by phone from Joyceville Institution.

Middleton, who told the inquest he stands six-footfour and weighs 300 pounds, said he tried to stop other inmates from bullying Geddes, who was drooling and talking incoherently on the pod. He said he was still traumatized by what happened and told jurors he was in tears as he testified.
"I believe that no one was unmoved by the testimony of Mr. Middleton. It's important to recognize the potential that this process can be traumatic and reopen old wounds," Wilson said.

"Nothing can replace the loss of a loved one. Having answers might, perhaps, provide a small amount of comfort. Recommendations that may reduce the chances of a reoccurrence can help with the process of grieving.
